items.title: Q1 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernism (1900–1945) · Unit I: Drama · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: G.B. Shaw's Pygmalion dramatizes the myth of a sculptor who fell in love with an ivory statue
items.explanation: George Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion (1913) is based on the ancient Greek myth of Pygmalion (recounted in Ovid's Metamorphoses), a Cypriot sculptor who falls in love with Galatea, an ivory statue he carved.

items.title: Q2 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit II: Poetry · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Empedocles on Etna is an example of
items.explanation: Matthew Arnold's Empedocles on Etna (1852) is a dramatic poem and closet drama in two acts exploring the philosophical isolation of the Greek philosopher Empedocles before he leaps into the crater of Mount Etna.

items.title: Q3 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration & Augustan Age · Unit I: Drama · William Congreve
items.stem: Which of the following description of characters from William Congreve's The Way of the World is incorrect?
options: Fainall, in love with Mrs. Marwood
Mirabell, in love with Mrs. Millamant
items.explanation: In the Dramatis Personae of William Congreve's Restoration comedy The Way of the World (1700), both Witwoud and Petulant are described as followers of Mrs. Millamant, not Mrs. Marwood.

items.title: Q4 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
The following lines are spoken by which character in Shakespeare's plays?
Put out the light, and then put out the light:
If I quench thee, thou flaming minister,
I can again thy former light restore
items.explanation: Othello speaks these famous lines in Act V, Scene 2 of Shakespeare's Othello (c. 1603–1604) as he enters Desdemona's bedchamber holding a candle just before extinguishing her life.

items.title: Q5 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter
items.stem: Which of the following settings of Harold Pinter's play The Birthday Party is incorrect?
options: ACT I- A morning in winter
ACT II- Evening of the same day
items.explanation: In Harold Pinter's comedy of menace The Birthday Party (1958), the living room of Meg and Petey Boles's seaside boarding house is set on a morning in summer in Act I, the evening of the same day in Act II, and the next morning in Act III.

items.title: Q6 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: In which of the following novels of Charles Dickens, the city of London is shown shrouded in fog in the opening chapter?
items.explanation: Charles Dickens's Bleak House (1852–1853) famously opens in Chapter 1 ('In Chancery') with a dense fog enveloping London and the High Court of Chancery, symbolizing the obscurity and corruption of the legal system.

items.title: Q7 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jane Austen, George Orwell, Aldous Huxley, William Golding
items.stem: Which of the following novels is not an example of dystopian novel?
options: William Golding's Lord of the Flies
items.explanation: Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice (1813) is a romantic novel of manners set in Regency England, whereas Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), Brave New World (1932), and Lord of the Flies (1954) are classic dystopian fictions.

items.title: Q8 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Which of the following novels is not the part of Samuel Beckett's trilogy published together in London in 1959?
items.explanation: Samuel Beckett's postwar trilogy published in English in one volume in 1959 consists of Molloy (1951), Malone Dies (1951), and The Unnamable (1953); Murphy (1938) is an earlier standalone novel.

items.title: Q9 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernism (1900–1945) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · E. M. Forster
items.stem: Which of the following novels of E. M. Forster doesn't display the mentioned contrast?
options: Contrast of East and West in A Passage to India
Contrast of English and French culture in Where Angels Fear to Tread
Contrast of English and Italian culture in A Room with a View
Contrast of the Schlegels and the Wilcoxes families in Howards End
items.explanation: E. M. Forster's debut novel Where Angels Fear to Tread (1905) contrasts repressed English suburban culture (Sawston) with passionate Italian culture (Monteriano), rather than French culture.

items.title: Q10 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charlotte Brontë
items.stem:
Identify the novelist who wrote the following lines; and to whom is it written?
"In delineating male character, I labour under disadvantages; intuition and theory will not adequately supply the place of observation and experience. When I write about women, I am sure of my ground—in the other case I am not so sure."
options: Charlotte Brontë wrote to James Taylor
Jane Austen wrote to Elizabeth Sewell
Margaret Oliphant wrote to Isabella Blackwood
Charlotte Yonge wrote to Felicia Skene
items.explanation: Charlotte Brontë wrote these lines in a letter dated March 1, 1849 to James Taylor of her publishing house Smith, Elder & Co., reflecting on the difficulty of portraying male characters while writing Shirley.

items.title: Q11 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: In English, if three consonants form a cluster at the beginning of a syllable, the first consonant will be always
items.explanation: In English, a three-consonant cluster at the start of a syllable (as in 'split', 'street', 'screen') always begins with /s/, followed by a stop and then a liquid or glide.

items.title: Q12 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: What do we call the space between the vocal folds?
items.explanation: In articulatory phonetics, the glottis is the anatomical opening or space between the vocal folds (vocal cords) located inside the larynx.

items.title: Q13 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following is an example of Functional Morpheme?
items.explanation: A functional morpheme is a free word that does a grammatical job, like 'and', 'the' or 'in'. 'Teach' is a lexical morpheme, while '-er' and '-ed' are bound morphemes.

items.title: Q14 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following definitions of various social variation in language is incorrect?
options: Convergence is a speech style that attempts to reduce social distance, and use forms that are similar to those used by the person we are talking to.
A register is a conventional way of using language that is appropriate in a specific context, which may be identified as situational, occupational or topical.
Slang describes words or phrases that are used instead of more everyday terms among younger speakers and other groups with special interests.
Jargons are words and phrases, often involving body parts, bodily functions and sexual acts, that people avoid for reasons related to religion, politeness and prohibited behavior.
items.explanation: In George Yule's The Study of Language, words and phrases avoided for reasons of religion, politeness, or prohibited behavior are defined as taboo terms, whereas jargon refers to specialized technical vocabulary used by a specific profession or group.

items.title: Q15 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Ferdinand de Saussure
items.stem: Which of the following descriptions of arbitrary nature of the sign given by Ferdinand de Saussure in his book Course in General Linguistics is incorrect?
options: The bond between the signifier and the signified is arbitrary
The word symbol has been used to designate the linguistic meaning or more specifically, the signified
Symbol is never wholly arbitrary; it is not empty, for there is the rudiment of a natural bond between the signifier and the signified
items.explanation: In Course in General Linguistics (1916), Ferdinand de Saussure states that the word 'symbol' has been used to designate the linguistic sign, or more specifically the signifier, rather than the signified.

items.title: Q16 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Jayanta Mahapatra
items.stem: Whose poetry is redolent of the Orissa scene and the Jagannatha temple at Puri figures quite often in it?
items.explanation: Jayanta Mahapatra's poetry is deeply rooted in the landscape and cultural memory of Odisha, with the Jagannatha temple at Puri figuring prominently in poems such as 'Dawn at Puri' and Relationship (1980).

items.title: Q17 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Girish Karnad, Thomas Mann
items.stem: Girish Karnad's Hayavadana and Thomas Mann's short novel, The Transposed Heads, are based on the tale of
items.explanation: Girish Karnad's play Hayavadana (1971) and Thomas Mann's novella The Transposed Heads (1940) are both adapted from a Sanskrit tale in the Vetala Panchavimshati found within Somadeva's 11th-century Kathasaritsagara.

items.title: Q18 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Anita Desai
items.stem: In which novel of Anita Desai, the heroine, in her fifth pregnancy, leaves her husband in a mood of unease to seek peace in an island, Manori, off Bombay?
options: Where shall we go this Summer
items.explanation: In Anita Desai's novel Where Shall We Go This Summer? (1975), the protagonist Sita, distressed during her fifth pregnancy, leaves her husband Raman in Bombay to seek refuge on the island of Manori.

items.title: Q19 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Nirad C. Chaudhuri
items.stem: Which of the following books has an account of the 'Adventures of a Brown Man in Search of Civilization'?
items.explanation: Nirad C. Chaudhuri's travelogue A Passage to England (1959), chronicling his first five-week visit to Britain at age fifty-seven, is famously described by M. K. Naik as the 'Adventures of a Brown Man in Search of Civilization'.

items.title: Q20 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Sharankumar Limbale
items.stem: Which of the following is not one of the conceptions of dalit aesthetics given by Sharankumar Limbale?
options: Human beings are first and foremost human – this is satyam
The liberation of human beings is shivam
The humanity of human beings is sundaram
The equality, liberty, justice and fraternity of human beings are satyam and sundaram
items.explanation: In Towards an Aesthetic of Dalit Literature (2004), Sharankumar Limbale redefines the aesthetic triad as: human beings are first and foremost human (Satyam), the liberation of human beings is Shivam, and the humanity of human beings is Sundaram.

items.title: Q21 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Fiona Tolan
items.stem: Fiona Tolan in "Feminisms" says that if there is a single identifiable theme running through every feminist debate, it is the question of
items.explanation: In her chapter 'Feminisms' (in Patricia Waugh's Literary Theory and Criticism), Fiona Tolan argues that the question of essentialism—whether a universal female nature exists—is the single identifiable theme running through every feminist debate.

items.title: Q22 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Jeremy Hawthorn
items.stem: According to Jeremy Hawthorn, which of the following can be said to "have prepared the ground for the development of theories of the gaze"?
options: Michael Argyle and Mark Cook's Gaze and Mutual Gaze
Sigmund Freud's Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality
Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison
items.explanation: In A Glossary of Contemporary Literary Theory, Jeremy Hawthorn observes that John Berger's Ways of Seeing (1972) prepared the ground for feminist and film theories of the gaze by showing how men look at women while women watch themselves being looked at.

items.title: Q23 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · John Fiske
items.stem: Who has insisted that the power of the audience "derives from the fact that meanings do not circulate in the cultural economy in the same way that wealth does in the financial"?
items.explanation: In Television Culture (1987), media theorist John Fiske argues that the active audience's semiotic power derives from the fact that meanings circulate in the cultural economy differently from wealth in the financial economy.

items.title: Q24 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Angela McRobbie
items.stem: Angela McRobbie, in an influential essay first published in 1978, argues that Jackie, the best-selling teenage girls' magazine in the 1970s, can be analysed "as a system of messages, a signifying system and a bearer of a certain ideology, an ideology which deals with the construction of teenage femininity". McRobbie identifies four strategies ('subcodes') through which Jackie makes its appeal. Identify the correct strategies or subcodes given below
options: The code of cinema, the code of personal/domestic life, the code of fashion and beauty and the code of pop music
The code of romance, the code of personal/domestic life, the code of fashion and beauty and the code of Mall-Culture
The code of romance, the code of personal/domestic life, the code of fashion and beauty and the code of pop music
The code of cinema, the code of personal/domestic life, the code of cosmetics and beauty and the code of pop music
items.explanation: In her 1978 Birmingham Centre essay on the teenage girls' magazine Jackie, Angela McRobbie identifies four ideological subcodes constructing teenage femininity: the code of romance, the code of personal/domestic life, the code of fashion and beauty, and the code of pop music.

items.title: Q25 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams
items.stem: Who defined culture as "one of the two or three most complicated words in the English language"?
items.explanation: In Keywords: A Vocabulary of Culture and Society (1976), Welsh cultural materialist critic Raymond Williams famously opens his entry on 'Culture' by calling it one of the two or three most complicated words in the English language.

items.title: Q26 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Peter Gay
items.stem:
Who wrote the following about Rousseau?
"Like his favorite philosopher, Plato, Rousseau sought to discover and produce the moral man who would make the moral society, and a moral society that would foster the moral man."
items.explanation: Enlightenment historian Peter Gay wrote this assessment of Jean-Jacques Rousseau in The Enlightenment: An Interpretation (1969), comparing Rousseau's dual project in Emile and The Social Contract to Plato's Republic.

items.title: Q27 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical & Ancient Background · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Horace
items.stem: Which of the following issues is not focussed by Horace in his Ars Poetica?
options: The detachment of a writer to his work, tradition, and custom
The moral and social functions of poetry
The contribution of an audience to the composition of poetry
An awareness of literary history and historical change in language and genre
items.explanation: In his Ars Poetica (c. 19 BCE), Horace emphasizes poetic decorum, adherence to classical tradition and custom, the moral and social functions of poetry (dulce et utile), audience reception, and historical change in language, rather than detachment from tradition.

items.title: Q28 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: In 1832, at the end of what is now called the Romantic age, Samuel Taylor Coleridge described "three silent revolutions in England". Identify the wrong option
options: When the Professions fell off from the Church
When the fraternity fell off from the society
When Literature fell off from the Professions
When the Press fell off from Literature
items.explanation: In Table Talk (1832), Samuel Taylor Coleridge identified three silent revolutions in England: when the Professions fell off from the Church, when Literature fell off from the Professions, and when the Press fell off from Literature.

items.title: Q29 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Which of the following critical works of Matthew Arnold does preach that "The Kingdom of God is within you"?
items.explanation: Literature and Dogma (1873) is Arnold's work on religion and the Bible. It argues that true religion is inner righteousness and conduct, which echoes 'The Kingdom of God is within you'.

items.title: Q30 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Johann Gottfried von Herder, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Friedrich Schiller
items.stem: Johann Gottfried von Herder, Goethe, and Schiller experimented with new subjective modes of expression; which movement/circle did they belong to?
items.explanation: Johann Gottfried von Herder, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, and Friedrich Schiller were central figures of the late 18th-century German Sturm und Drang ('Storm and Stress') movement, which championed emotional subjectivity and individual expression.

items.title: Q31 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jean Baudrillard
items.stem: Who became known in the popular imagination as the notorious French postmodernist philosopher?
items.explanation: French theorist Jean Baudrillard became known in popular imagination as the notorious French postmodernist philosopher for his provocative theories of hyperreality and simulation in Simulacra and Simulation (1981) and The Gulf War Did Not Take Place (1991).

items.title: Q32 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Jonathan Dollimore, Alan Sinfield
items.stem: Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield define the term "Cultural materialism" as designating a critical method having characteristics. Which of the following characteristics has not been included by Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield?
items.explanation: In their Foreword to Political Shakespeare (1985), Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield define cultural materialism through four characteristics—historical context, theoretical method, political commitment, and textual analysis—explicitly rejecting claims of timeless or transcendental significance.

items.title: Q33 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernism (1900–1945) · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Virginia Woolf
items.stem:
Which of the following feminists has questioned the following?
"Why did men drink wine and women water? Why was one sex so prosperous and the other so poor? What effect has poverty on fiction? What conditions are necessary for the creation of works of art?"
items.explanation: Virginia Woolf poses these famous questions in Chapter 1 of her feminist essay A Room of One's Own (1929), examining how material wealth, social privilege, and economic independence shape women's ability to write fiction.

items.title: Q34 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Ania Loomba
items.stem: Who amongst the following postcolonial critics did define colonialism "as the conquest and control of other people's land and goods"?
items.explanation: In Colonialism/Postcolonialism (1998), postcolonial critic Ania Loomba defines colonialism at its most basic level as 'the conquest and control of other people's land and goods.'

items.title: Q35 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Melanie Klein
items.stem: According to whom, "the interaction between introjection and projection helps to constitute the ego and the superego and to lay the foundations for the Oedipus complex"?
items.explanation: In object-relations psychoanalysis, Melanie Klein argued that the early infant psyche is structured by the continuous interaction between introjection and projection, which constitutes the ego and superego and lays the foundation for the Oedipus complex.

items.title: Q36 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Sigmund Freud
items.stem: According to Freud's example in his Interpretation of Dreams, the psychoanalytic critic tends to associate symbols with images. Which of the following symbols is not correct in that context?
options: Ponds as female or yonic symbols
Flowers as female or yonic symbols
Towers as symbols of sexual pleasure
Lances as male or phallic symbols
items.explanation: In Freudian dream symbolism as outlined in The Interpretation of Dreams (1899) and Wilfred L. Guerin's Handbook of Critical Approaches to Literature, towers, lances, and spires are male or phallic symbols, while ponds and flowers are female or yonic symbols.

items.title: Q37 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernism (1900–1945) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Northrop Frye
items.stem: Which of the following seasons does Northrop Frye, in his Anatomy of Criticism, not indicate the corresponding genres?
items.explanation: In the 'Theory of Myths' section of Anatomy of Criticism (1957), Northrop Frye names the four seasonal mythoi as the mythos of spring (comedy), summer (romance), autumn (tragedy), and winter (irony and satire), using 'autumn' rather than 'fall'.

items.title: Q38 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Elaine Showalter
items.stem: In which of the following phases of modern women's literary development, according to Elaine Showalter, 'women writers imitated the dominant male traditions'?
items.explanation: In A Literature of Their Own (1977), Elaine Showalter divides women's literary history into three stages: the Feminine phase (1840–1880), when women imitated dominant male traditions; the Feminist phase (1880–1920); and the Female phase (1920 onwards).

items.title: Q39 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Arrange the following list of the authors according to MLA Handbook 9th edition for parenthetical citations and works-cited-list entries:
Rita Charon
Sayantani Dasgupta
Nellie Hermann
Craig Irvine
Eric R. Marcus
Edgar Rivera Colon
Danielle Spencer
Maura Spiegel
options: Charon, Rita, and Dasgupta, et al.
Charon, Rita and Dasgupta, Hermann, Irvine, Marcus, Colon, Spencer, Spiegel.
items.explanation: MLA 9th edition: when a source has three or more authors, give only the first author followed by 'et al.' So 'Charon, Rita, et al.' is correct.

items.title: Q40 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which of the following in-text citations is incorrect?
options: Others note that doctors have not yet adequately explained the effects climate change will have on human health (Lemery and Auerbach 4–5).
According to Naomi Baron, reading is "just half of literacy. The other half is writing" (Baron 194).
According to Gao Xingjian, "Literature in essence is divorced from utility" (7).
The author knew Bureau de la Rivière, another of Charles V's executors (Christine 192).
items.explanation: According to the MLA Handbook (9th edition), when an author's name (Naomi Baron) is already stated in the signal phrase within the sentence, repeating the surname in the parenthetical citation '(Baron 194)' is redundant; it should simply be '(194)'.

items.title: Q41 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Medieval Period · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: The best-known cycles of miracle or mystery plays come from York, Wakefield, and Chester.
Reason R: King Alfred encouraged the use of the vernacular in the late ninth century, but he made it clear that this was very much second best, necessitated by the deplorably low standards of Latin learning in his kingdom.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: Both statements are historically accurate facts from Ronald Carter and John McRae's The Routledge History of Literature in English: the late medieval mystery play cycles came from York, Wakefield, and Chester, while King Alfred promoted Old English vernacular prose in the late ninth century, though R does not explain A.

items.title: Q42 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: The years after 1945 saw changes in English poetry.
Reason R: Some poets, despite Modernism, continued Romantic traditions, writing deeply personal responses to the world and engaging with 'eternal', 'elemental' themes.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: As noted in Carter and McRae's The Routledge History of Literature in English, post-1945 English poetry underwent significant shifts as Neo-Romantic poets like Dylan Thomas and George Barker continued Romantic traditions with deeply personal, elemental themes.

items.title: Q43 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Christopher Brookmyre
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: The defining event of the first part of the twenty-first century was the attack on American targets, including the Twin Towers in New York, on 11 September 2001.
Reason R: A novel by Christopher Brookmyre published two days before the attacks happened, A Big Boy Did It and Ran Away, was, and still is, astonishingly prescient both about the violence and about some of its roots and resonances.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: Both statements are true observations from Carter and McRae's The Routledge History of Literature in English regarding the September 11, 2001 attacks and Scottish novelist Christopher Brookmyre's prescient novel A Big Boy Did It and Ran Away (2001), though R is not the cause of A.

items.title: Q44 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: Bacon's position as an essayist is peculiar.
Reason R: He has no resemblance to Addison or Hazlitt.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: In The English Essay and Essayists (1915), Hugh Walker states that Francis Bacon's position as an essayist is peculiar because his aphoristic, impersonal counsel bears no stylistic resemblance to later familiar essayists like Joseph Addison or William Hazlitt.

items.title: Q45 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: All modern languages have some words with pronunciations that seem to echo naturally occurring sounds.
Reason R: When different objects flew by, making a caw-caw or coo-coo sound, the early human tried to imitate the sounds and then used them to refer to those objects even when they weren't present.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: In George Yule's The Study of Language, the 'bow-wow' hypothesis of the natural sound source explains that all modern languages contain onomatopoeic words echoing natural sounds because early humans imitated environmental sounds like 'caw-caw' or 'coo-coo' to refer to those objects.

items.title: Q46 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: A dozen or more distinct languages and literatures flourish today on the Indian literary scene, and most of these are distributed on a broadly regional basis.
Reason R: The Aryans brought Sanskrit to India; the Muslim rule led to the rise of Urdu, as an expression of a composite culture; and the British rule made Indo-Anglian literature possible.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: In K. R. Srinivasa Iyengar's Indian Writing in English, India's diverse regional and pan-Indian literary traditions are explained through historical waves: Sanskrit brought by the Aryans, Urdu emerging under Muslim rule, and Indo-Anglian literature enabled by British rule.

items.title: Q47 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Stuart Hall
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: Television is the popular cultural form of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.
Reason R: Meanings and messages are not simply 'transmitted', they are always produced: first by the encoder from the 'raw' material of everyday life; second by the audience in relation to its location in other discourses.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct

When I was fair and young, then favor graced me,
Of many was I sought their mistress for to be,
But I did scorn them all and answered them therefore:
Go, go, go, seek some other where, importune me no more.

How many weeping eyes I made to pine in woe,
How many sighing hearts I have not skill to show,
But I the prouder grew and still this spake therefore:
Go, go, go, seek some other where, importune me no more.

Then spake fair Venus' son, that proud victorious boy,
Saying: you dainty dame, for that you be so coy,
I will so pluck your plumes as you shall say no more:
Go, go, go, seek some other where, importune me no more.

As soon as he had said such change grew in my breast,
That neither night nor day I could take any rest,
Wherefore I did repent that I had said before:
Go, go, go, seek some other where, importune me no more.

She was very beautiful and young
She had the favour of many of her lovers
items.explanation: In the opening line of Queen Elizabeth I's lyric 'When I Was Fair and Young', 'fair and young' and 'favor graced me' connote that the speaker was blessed with youth, physical beauty, and comeliness that attracted many admirers.

items.title: Q96 · Jan 2026 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration & Augustan Age · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Joseph Addison
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions.

There is nothing that more betrays a base ungenerous spirit than the giving of secret stabs to a man's reputation; lampoons and satires that are written with wit and spirit are like poisoned darts, which not only inflict a wound, but make it incurable. For this reason I am very much troubled when I see the talents of humour and ridicule in the possession of an ill-natured man. There cannot be a greater gratification to a barbarous and inhuman wit than to stir up sorrow in the heart of a private person, to raise uneasiness among near relations, and to expose whole families to derision, at the same time that he remains unseen and undiscovered. If, besides the accomplishments of being witty and ill-natured, a man is vicious into the bargain, he is one of the most mischievous creatures that can enter into a civil society. His satire will then chiefly fall upon those who ought to be the most exempt from it. Virtue, merit, and everything, that is praiseworthy, will be made the subject of ridicule and buffoonery. It is impossible to enumerate the evils which arise from these arrow that fly in the dark; and I know no other excuse that is or can be made for them, than that the wounds they give are only imaginary, and produce nothing more than a secret shame or sorrow in the mind of the suffering person.

Question 96: In the passage, "secret stabs" stands for:
options: Poisoned darts which pricks and inflicts
items.explanation: In this passage from Joseph Addison's The Spectator (No. 23), 'the giving of secret stabs to a man's reputation' refers directly to malicious 'lampoons and satires that are written with wit and spirit' to wound a person covertly.
